clinicalPearls: C. trachomatis genital infection is the most prevalent bacterial STI worldwide and is reported more than any other infectious disease in the United States; case counts are heavily dependent on screening coverage (Harrison 22e p.1469).

Most genital infections are silent: up to 80-90% of women and >50% of men with C. trachomatis genital infection lack symptoms, and pharyngeal/rectal infection is typically asymptomatic and may persist for years, sustaining a large transmission reservoir (Harrison 22e p.1469).
C. trachomatis is the most common cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU) and postgonococcal urethritis (PGU), implicated in 30-50% of NGU cases (Harrison 22e p.1469-1470).

NAATs are the CDC-recommended diagnostic assay of choice; less-invasive specimens (urine for both sexes, vaginal swabs for women) are acceptable, and self-collected or clinician-collected vaginal swabs are slightly more sensitive than urine in women (Harrison 22e p.1472-1473).
Because of frequent co-infection, testing for or treating chlamydia should be considered in patients diagnosed with N. gonorrhoeae (Harrison 22e p.1474).

Trachoma (serovars A, B, Ba, C) remains a leading cause of preventable infectious blindness worldwide; the WHO SAFE-era programs target elimination as a public health problem by 2030 (Harrison 22e p.1474-1475).

LGV (serovars L1, L2, L3) is an invasive STI presenting classically as a transient painless genital ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy with bubo formation, or as hemorrhagic proctocolitis in MSM (Harrison 22e p.1469, 1472).

C. pneumoniae causes atypical (community-acquired) pneumonia, bronchitis, pharyngitis and sinusitis, accounting for as many as 10% of CAP cases though more typically 1-2%; PCR of respiratory secretions is the preferred diagnostic method (Harrison 22e p.1476).

Psittacosis (C. psittaci) is a zoonosis acquired from birds (psittacines, poultry) presenting as atypical pneumonia or systemic febrile illness; person-to-person transmission has never been demonstrated (Harrison 22e p.1475).

Neonatal exposure during vaginal delivery causes inclusion conjunctivitis (in ~20-30% of exposed infants) and, in 10-15%, pneumonia at 2 weeks to 4 months of age; standard gonococcal ocular prophylaxis does NOT prevent chlamydial conjunctivitis (Harrison 22e p.1471-1472).
harrison.pathophysiology: Chlamydiae are nonmotile, gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria that lack peptidoglycan (structural integrity depends on disulfide cross-linking of outer-membrane proteins) and are energy parasites using host-cell ATP. They have a unique biphasic growth cycle alternating between the infectious, extracellular-adapted elementary body (0.25-0.35 um) and the metabolically active, non-infectious intracellular reticulate body (0.5-1 um), which divides by binary fission within a membrane-bound cytoplasmic inclusion while preventing phagosome-lysosome fusion; the cycle lasts ~48-72 h, giving a long clinical incubation (generally 1-3 weeks). C. trachomatis has two biovars (trachoma and LGV) and 18 serovars (trachoma A/B/Ba/C; oculogenital D-K; LGV L1-L3); the trachoma biovar parasitizes squamocolumnar epithelium whereas the more invasive LGV biovar involves lymphoid cells. Disease is driven largely by immunopathology rather than direct cytotoxicity: the chlamydial heat-shock protein shares epitopes with human and other bacterial proteins and, with repeated/persistent infection, drives fibrosis and mucosal scarring leading to tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy and chronic pelvic pain (genital) or cicatricial trichiasis and blindness (ocular). Antigenic variation in the major outer-membrane protein (omp1) permits reinfection because immunity to one serovar is not protective against others (Harrison 22e p.1467-1469).
additionalDifferentials: Neisseria gonorrhoeae urethritis/cervicitis/proctitis (clinically indistinguishable; frequent co-infection)
Mycoplasma genitalium (now a leading cause of Chlamydia-negative and persistent NGU)
Trichomonas vaginalis and herpes simplex virus as causes of NGU
Mycoplasma pneumoniae and other atypical pneumonia pathogens (for C. pneumoniae)
Crohn's disease of the rectum (mimicked by LGV proctocolitis on sigmoidoscopy and histology)
Adenovirus or HSV follicular conjunctivitis (mimics adult inclusion/oculogenital conjunctivitis)
infectionMimics: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (urethritis, cervicitis, PID, proctitis, ophthalmia neonatorum)
Herpes simplex virus (urethritis, proctitis, ulcerative conjunctivitis)
Haemophilus influenzae or Streptococcus pneumoniae neonatal conjunctivitis
Mycoplasma pneumoniae and other atypical CAP agents (for C. pneumoniae pneumonia)
Haemophilus ducreyi and other genital-ulcer pathogens (for LGV primary lesion)
nonInfectiousMimics: Crohn's disease of the rectum (resembles LGV/serovar proctocolitis: granulomas, giant cells, crypt abscesses)
Testicular torsion or testicular tumor (mimic chlamydial epididymitis; torsion must be excluded promptly)
Functional urinary symptoms / non-infectious dysuria (acute urethral syndrome in women)
Reactive arthritis / spondyloarthropathy in the differential of HLA-B27-associated joint disease
additionalInvestigations: NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) on urine, vaginal/cervical, urethral, rectal, pharyngeal or conjunctival specimens - diagnostic assay of choice
First-void urine or vaginal swab self-collection for screening programs and outreach
Microscopy for leukocytes (Gram stain of urethral exudate or cervical mucus; first-void urine pyuria; leukocyte esterase) to support presumptive diagnosis of urethritis/cervicitis
Giemsa-stained smears for intracytoplasmic inclusions (conjunctival scrapings, neonatal specimens; less sensitive than NAAT/culture)
Microimmunofluorescence (MIF) serology - test of choice for LGV and neonatal pneumonia and the serologic gold standard, though labor-intensive and largely research-only
Complement fixation (CF) serology (genus-level only via LPS; fourfold titer rise supports psittacosis)
PCR of respiratory secretions for C. pneumoniae (preferred) and respiratory NAAT for C. psittaci
Cell culture (former gold standard) - now performed only in specialized laboratories
Sigmoidoscopy with rectal biopsy for proctitis/LGV (granulomas, crypt abscesses)
Laparoscopy / endometrial biopsy (plasma-cell endometritis) in suspected salpingitis/PID and perihepatitis
Serovar/molecular genotyping when LGV is suspected (longer treatment duration required)
redFlags: Acute unilateral testicular pain - exclude testicular torsion promptly by imaging or surgical exploration before attributing to epididymitis
Failure of unilateral intrascrotal pain/swelling to respond to antimicrobials - exclude testicular tumor or chronic infection such as tuberculosis
Hemorrhagic proctocolitis with severe anorectal pain in MSM - consider invasive LGV serovars (often with HIV co-infection)
Right-upper-quadrant pain/fever/nausea in a sexually active woman - suspect perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis), associated with extensive tubal scarring
Trichiasis and entropion in trachoma - lashes abrade the cornea leading to ulceration and blindness if untreated
Severe psittacosis pneumonia - can be fatal in up to 10% of untreated cases and may require ICU care, with hepatitis, endocarditis or myocarditis
Untreated maternal infection - risk of neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis and infant pneumonia
harrison.prognosis: Uncomplicated genital chlamydial infection responds well to recommended antibiotics, and clinically significant drug resistance has not been observed in C. trachomatis; apparent treatment failure usually reflects non-adherence or reinfection. However, untreated or recurrent genital infection causes substantial long-term morbidity through mucosal scarring - PID with tubal-factor infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain - and women bear the greatest burden of sequelae. Reactive arthritis episodes typically last 2-6 months. Untreated ocular disease progresses to blinding trachoma; the WHO estimates ~6 million people have been blinded and ~1.3 million remain blind from trachoma. Untreated psittacosis pneumonia can be fatal in up to 10% of cases. Previous chlamydial infection raises the risk of reinfection, prompting rescreening at 3 months (Harrison 22e p.1469-1475).
pitfalls: NAATs detect nucleic acid, not viable organisms - residual DNA may yield a positive result for up to 3 weeks after effective therapy, so NAATs should not be used as a test of cure before 3 weeks; routine test of cure is not recommended except in pregnancy.
Single-dose penicillins or cephalosporins used for gonorrhea lack activity against chlamydiae - hence postgonococcal urethritis and the need to co-treat or exclude chlamydia.
Standard gonococcal ocular prophylaxis does NOT prevent neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis; the most effective prevention is antenatal screening and treatment.
Chlamydial and gonococcal conjunctivitis cannot be distinguished from other neonatal conjunctivitis on clinical grounds - laboratory diagnosis is required.
CF and LPS-based serologic tests identify chlamydiae only to the genus level (cross-reactive across all chlamydiae) and must be interpreted cautiously.
Serology (including a single high IgG titer) over-attributes C. pneumoniae to atypical pneumonia; cross-reactivity limits specificity, and PCR is preferred.
Serology is never recommended for diagnosis of uncomplicated genital cervical/urethral/lower-tract infection or for asymptomatic screening.
Fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in pregnancy; beta-lactams and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are not active against C. pneumoniae.
Most genital infections are asymptomatic, so clinical recognition of cervicitis requires a high index of suspicion - no genital symptom is specific for chlamydial cervical infection.
C. psittaci is a biohazard category B biothreat agent associated with laboratory-acquired infections.
harrison.severityClassification: No formal grading scale. Genital C. trachomatis infections are categorized as uncomplicated (lower genital tract) versus complicated (e.g., PID, epididymitis) requiring longer therapy; LGV is treated as invasive disease with extended therapy. Trachoma is described by phase - active trachoma (follicular conjunctivitis) versus cicatricial disease (conjunctival scarring, trichiasis, entropion) - underpinning the WHO clinical signs used for diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1474-1475).
management: First-line antimicrobial therapy with doxycycline of the tetracycline class for uncomplicated genital infection, with azithromycin of the macrolide class as an alternative
A prolonged tetracycline course for lymphogranuloma venereum, and a macrolide such as erythromycin or azithromycin in pregnancy and for neonatal disease
Partner notification, testing and treatment, with abstinence until therapy is complete to prevent reinfection
Test for co-infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and other sexually transmitted infections including HIV
Retest for reinfection at follow-up given the high reinfection rate, and perform a test of cure in pregnancy
Treat neonatal ophthalmia neonatorum and chlamydial pneumonia with a systemic macrolide
For trachoma, apply the WHO SAFE strategy of lid surgery, mass azithromycin administration, facial cleanliness and environmental improvement
Public health notification and participation in screening programmes to reduce the transmission reservoir
